Emergence of a monopole phase in the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice for small magnetic fields

Sasank Budaraju Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Shi Feng Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Josef Willsher Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für Physik komplexer Systeme, Nöthnitzer Strasse 38, 01187 Dresden, Germany    Johannes Knolle Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany Affiliation: Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom    Frank Pollmann Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Federico Becca Affiliation: Dipartimento di Fisica, Università di Trieste, Strada Costiera 11, I-34151 Trieste, Italy
Abstract

We investigate the ground-state phase diagram of the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice under an external Zeeman field HH by using the variational Monte Carlo approach. We span a region with 0≤J2/J1≤0.20\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.2 and 0≤H/J1≤20\leq H/J_{1}\leq 2, to assess the fate of the (putative) spin-liquid phase that has been detected for J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8 at zero magnetic field. Simple variational ansätze are proposed for a few candidate states, and their energetics are compared on large clusters to obtain the phase diagram. For J2/J1≲1/6J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1/6, a continuous transition from a gapless “Y” phase to a gapped “up-up-down” phase is obtained, as predicted by spin-wave theory. Most importantly, around J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8, a condensate of monopoles (which are gapless gauge excitations of the spin liquid at H=0H=0) is stabilized in a significant region of the phase diagram, for small Zeeman fields. Here, a finite scalar chirality is present, while no transverse magnetic order is detected. The stability of the monopole phase is confirmed by a field-theory approach that includes a self-consistent random-phase approximation of the low-lying spin fluctuations. The boundary between the monopole and “Y” phases is also obtained with no free parameters.

I Introduction

Triangular lattice antiferromagnets have been a birthplace for key ideas in condensed matter, such as frustrated magnetism and the existence of quantum spin liquids. The latter ones represent exotic states of matter that avoid spontaneous symmetry breaking even at zero temperature and feature emergent gauge fields and fractionalized degrees of freedom [35, 51, 28]. It has been suggested that the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model hosts a quantum spin liquid around J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8, although its nature is debated [52, 23, 24, 22, 13, 26, 11, 46, 25, 29]. In particular, variational Monte Carlo techniques suggested that the so-called U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac state represents a plausible candidate to describe the ground state in the highly-frustrated regime, i.e., 0.08≲J2/J1≲0.160.08\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.16 [24]. The low-energy description of this phase is given by massless fermions (spinons) with a cone-like dispersion (i.e., two Dirac points per spin species) interacting with a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field [13, 39, 45], which allows for monopole excitations because of its compact nature [17, 43, 19, 20, 18]. In this regard, recent studies have explored the possibility of stable monopoles that do not trigger confinement [32], focusing on their quantum numbers [39, 38, 14]. Numerical calculations have also been considered, supporting the possibility that monopoles are gapless in the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid [8].

The external magnetic field represents a standard experimental probe in solid-state physics, often used to probe the susceptibilities of the ground state in the absence of external perturbations. In the case of the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model, the external magnetic field is crucial in several aspects. From a purely theoretical side, it allows us to assess the stability of the Dirac spin liquid against the development of long-range magnetic correlations or other kinds of classical order. For example, a transverse 120∘120^{\circ} order may settle, as speculated from theoretical analysis [33] and supported by a recent Schwinger-boson mean-field approach [10]. On the practical side, quantitative estimations for the magnetization curve act as an experimental reference to quantify the proximity of a material to the ideal model.

The J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model with an external magnetic field HH has recently received considerable attention. In fact, linear spin-wave calculations [50, 49] have highlighted the existence of several semi-classical phases, with different spin patterns. More recently, spin-wave calculations have been pushed beyond the linear approximation and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) simulations have been implemented on relatively large clusters [4, 27]; here, a rich phase diagram has been obtained (with some differences between the two works), with evidence that an exotic phase (i.e., not captured by the semi-classical approximation) may exist around J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8 for small magnetic fields, below the m=1/3m=1/3 magnetization plateau.

Driven by theoretical advances, the search for quantum materials capable of reaching the J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} window required to have a quantum spin liquid has been carried out [30]. For example, AYbSe2{\rm AYbSe_{2}} (with A=Cs,K,Na{\rm A=Cs,K,Na}) and YbZn2​GaO5{\rm YbZn_{2}GaO_{5}} represent prominent candidates [36, 47, 5]; they host Yb3+{\rm Yb^{3+}} pseudo-spin-1/2 moments on isotropic triangular lattices where Heisenberg exchange is dominant. Despite their potential, determining the actual value of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} is difficult. For example, calculations for AYbSe2{\rm AYbSe_{2}} using nonlinear spin-wave theory on the m=1/3m=1/3 plateau suggest J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} ratios between 0.030.03 and 0.070.07, which may not be enough to reach the spin-liquid regime.

In this work, we present a detailed investigation of the phase diagram of the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model with an external magnetic field, in the regime 0≤H/J1≤20\leq H/J_{1}\leq 2. In particular, we employ the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) technique based on Gutzwiller-projected fermionic partons [24, 8]. Our motivation is two-fold: the first one is to obtain an accurate description (using simple variational wave functions) of the conventional ordered states (e.g. Y and canted stripe) that appear in the phase diagram [41] and evaluate their region of stability. The second and most important one is to clarify the fate of the Dirac spin liquid when an external field is added to the Heisenberg Hamiltonian. To do this, we extend the construction to include semi-classical phases that appear in the spin-wave approach. For example, the so-called “Y phase” (suitable for J2/J1≲1/8J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1/8), the “canted stripe phase” (suitable for 1/8≲J2/J1≲11/8\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1), and the “up-up-down phase” (suitable for the m=1/3m=1/3 plateau). In addition, the “umbrella phase” is also considered, as well as a more exotic “monopole phase”, which is constructed by adding a finite density of magnetic fluxes to the underlying Dirac spin liquid.

In the zero-field quantum spin liquid, the monopoles lead to critical fluctuations of competing order parameters, and organize the potential instabilities of the gapless spin liquid [20, 18, 39, 37]. In this work, we examine the possibility that the spin liquid develops a condensate of monopole fluxes under applying an external field HH, gapping the Dirac cones into emergent spinon Landau levels and confining the gauge degrees of freedom. This effect was proposed by Ran  et al. [33] to lead to a symmetry-broken state with in-plane magnetic order on the kagome lattice, but recent works on the triangular lattice have brought this picture into question [27, 4, 42].

The main results of this work are summarized in the phase diagram of Fig. 1. We observe a large portion of the phase diagram where a monopole phase is stabilized over semiclassical ordered states, and first-order transitions to neighboring Y and canted stripe orders. Overall, our results are in good agreement with recent spin-wave theory and DMRG calculations [27] on both the extent of the various phases and the nature of phase transitions between them, giving support to our approach. We would like to remark that the present phase diagram is built from calculations on a finite cluster, without a size-scaling analysis; for this reason, the spin-liquid region at H=0H=0 is underestimated with respect to the actual values obtained in Ref. [24]. The remarkable outcome is that the monopole phase gives the best variational ansatz in the highly-frustrated regime and for small external fields and hence represents the natural evolution of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid when the external magnetic field is switched on.

We bolster this picture with a complementary analytic calculation of the collective spin excitations in the monopole phase. Within this approach, the monopole phase is stable up to a critical field, above which the semiclassical Y order sets in. These results are in good agreement with our numerical calculations.

Finally, we discuss the scaling of the transverse structure factor and in-plane order with magnetic field and system size at different points in the phase diagram. This points to an extended, gapless monopole phase, with an absence of transverse magnetic order in the thermodynamic limit. Although further refinements to the variational wave function may yield lower variational energies (with possibly different physical properties), the present results provide a critical benchmark for future studies, also stimulating a reexamination of field-theoretical frameworks.

The rest of our paper is organized as follows: in section II, we describe the variational wave functions used to represent the various phases in the phase diagram. In section III, we present the VMC results, including the magnetization curves for a few values of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and the properties of the monopole phase. In section IV we present a field theoretical description of the collective modes in the monopole phase and provide theoretical calculations for the critical field HcH_{c} for the transition to the Y phase. Finally, we give some concluding remarks in section V.

II Parton construction of competing phases

We consider the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice, coupled to an external magnetic field along the zz direction:

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,k⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒k−H​∑iSiz,{\cal H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,k\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{k}-H\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}, (1)

where 𝐒i=(Six,Siy,Siz)\mathbf{S}_{i}=(S^{x}_{i},S^{y}_{i},S^{z}_{i}) is the spin 1/2 operator on site ii and ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\rangle and ⟨⟨…⟩⟩\langle\langle\dots\rangle\rangle denote nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor bonds, respectively. Periodic-boundary conditions are taken on clusters defined by 𝐓1=L​𝐚1\mathbf{T}_{1}=L\mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐓2=L​𝐚2\mathbf{T}_{2}=L\mathbf{a}_{2} [with 𝐚1=(1,0)\mathbf{a}_{1}=(1,0) and 𝐚2=(1/2,3/2)\mathbf{a}_{2}=(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2)]. Then, the total number of sites is N=L2N=L^{2}. Notice that, in presence of a finite magnetic field HH, the Hamiltonian has only the U⁡(1)U(1) (global) spin symmetry, i.e., it is invariant with respect to rotations along the zz-axis. This leads to the fact that [ℋ,Sz]=0[{\cal H},S^{z}]=0, with Sz=∑iSizS^{z}=\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}.

In the following, we explore the phase diagram of the Hamiltonian (1) by constructing variational ansätze for several phases. For that, the first step is to express the spin operator in terms of fermionic degrees of freedom (so-called partons):

Siα=12​∑τ,τ′ci,τ†​στ,τ′α​ci,τ′,S^{\alpha}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{i,\tau}\sigma^{\alpha}_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\tau^{\prime}}, (2)

where α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z and (σx,σy,σz)(\sigma^{x},\sigma^{y},\sigma^{z}) are Pauli matrices; the parton operators satisfy the anti-commutation relations {ci,τ,cj,τ′†}=δi,j​δτ,τ′\{c_{i,\tau},c^{\dagger}_{j,\tau^{\prime}}\}=\delta_{i,j}\delta_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}. This rewriting preserves the S​U​(2)SU(2) commutation relations of the original spin operators, and is exact if the constraint of one fermion per site is enforced. It also introduces a local S​U​(2)SU(2) gauge degree of freedom [1], which enables us to distinguish between different spin liquid states through the projective symmetry group classification [43, 44].

Then, a tight-binding (auxiliary) Hamiltonian for the partons is formulated, with variational parameters optimized to minimize the energy of the physical Hamiltonian (1). The generic form of this auxiliary Hamiltonian consists of a kinetic hopping term and a site-dependent fictitious magnetic field:

ℋaux=∑⟨i​j⟩,τti​j​ci,τ†​cj,τ+h.c.+∑i𝐌i⋅𝐒i,{\cal H}_{\text{aux}}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\tau}t_{ij}c^{\dagger}_{i,\tau}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\tau}+\text{h.c.}+\sum_{i}\mathbf{M}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{i}, (3)

where hopping parameters {ti​j}\{t_{ij}\} include specific signs/phases to include the orbital effects of fictitious (local) magnetic fields [21]; the spin operators must be thought of as expressed by Eq. (2).

Specifically, we consider four families of variational wave functions, denoted as Y, umbrella, canted stripe, and monopole. The former two have a three-sublattice unit cell, whereas the third one has a two-sublattice unit cell; the monopole states break all lattice symmetries on finite clusters and, therefore, have a unit cell as large as the lattice itself [8]. The details of these ansätze are given below.

Diagonalizing the auxiliary Hamiltonian ℋaux{\cal H}_{\text{aux}} yields the single-particle orbitals. Then, the many-body state |Φ⟩\ket{\Phi} is defined by filling the NN lowest-energy levels. In general, |Φ⟩\ket{\Phi} has a non-zero overlap with configurations containing zero or two fermions on one or more sites. The constraint of one fermion per site is achieved by applying the Gutzwiller projector:

𝒫G=∏i(ni,↑−ni,↓)2,{\cal P}_{G}=\prod_{i}(n_{i,\uparrow}-n_{i,\downarrow})^{2}, (4)

where ni,τ=ci,τ†​ci,τn_{i,\tau}=c^{\dagger}_{i,\tau}c_{i,\tau}. Furthermore, the presence of a generic field 𝐌i\mathbf{M}_{i} may mix the spin flavors in the tight-binding model, so that the resulting ground state |Φ⟩\ket{\Phi} will not have a well defined quantum number mm for the total spin component SzS^{z}. In our simulations, we choose to work with states that have a well defined magnetization, because this is a conserved quantity of the Hamiltonian (1). Therefore, we include a projector to a specific sector with

m=2​SzN,m=\frac{2S^{z}}{N}, (5)

yielding finally the variational wave function:

|Ψ⟩=𝒫m​𝒫G​|Φ⟩.\ket{\Psi}={\cal P}_{m}{\cal P}_{G}\ket{\Phi}. (6)

We emphasize that the projectors 𝒫m{\cal P}_{m} and 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} are enforced exactly in the Monte Carlo simulation by sampling only the subspace spanned by the allowed configurations (e.g., configurations with one fermion per site, with Sz=N​m/2S^{z}=Nm/2) [40, 6].

We now elaborate on the specific form of ti​jt_{ij} and 𝐌i\mathbf{M}_{i} for each of the states mentioned above. They can be thought of as modifications of the Dirac spin liquid ansatz, which has π\pi flux on each rhomboidal plaquette (i.e., 00 and π\pi fluxes on upward and downward triangular plaquettes or vice versa) [24]. Aside from the monopole states, all other states retain this Dirac [0,π][0,\pi] flux structure.

  1. 1.

    Y state: the hoppings ti​jt_{ij} are purely real, and their amplitudes are non-uniform, modulated according to Fig. 2(a). The fictitious fields 𝐌i\mathbf{M}_{i} are chosen to be different for each of the A, B, and C sublattices of the triangular lattice:

    𝐌i={(0,0,h1)if ​i∈A,(h2,0,−h3)if ​i∈B,(−h2,0,−h3)if ​i∈C.\mathbf{M}_{i}=\begin{cases}(0,0,h_{1})&\text{if }i\in A,\\ (h_{2},0,-h_{3})&\text{if }i\in B,\\ (-h_{2},0,-h_{3})&\text{if }i\in C.\\ \end{cases} (7)

    The angles among the three spins on each sublattice depend on the values of the three fields h1h_{1}, h2h_{2}, and h3h_{3} (still, the projections 𝒫m{\cal P}_{m} and 𝒫G{\cal P}_{G} may affect the angles obtained at the non-interacting level). In particular, h2=0h_{2}=0 yields the collinear up-up-down (UUD) state. We remark that the projector 𝒫m{\cal P}_{m} ensures that the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry of the Hamiltonian is not broken on any finite lattice, although the Y phase is super-solid [41]. The parameters h1h_{1}, h2h_{2}, h3h_{3}, and Δ\Delta are optimized.

  2. 2.

    Umbrella state: the hoppings ti​jt_{ij} are purely real, whose amplitudes |ti​j||t_{ij}| are translationally invariant. The fictitious magnetic field field is given by

    𝐌i=h⁡[cos⁡(𝐊⋅𝐑i),sin⁡(𝐊⋅𝐑i),0],\mathbf{M}_{i}=h\ [\cos(\mathbf{K} \cdot\mathbf{R}_i),\sin(\mathbf{K} \cdot\mathbf{R}_i),0], (8)

    where 𝐊=(4​π/3,0)\mathbf{K}=(4\pi/3,0) and hh is a variational parameter [24]. Performing a projection to a specific SzS^{z} sector gives a uniform zz component for all spins. The parameter hh is optimized.

  3. 3.

    Canted-stripe state: the hoppings ti​jt_{ij} are purely real and their amplitudes are modulated according to Fig. 2(b). The fictitious field again has the form:

    OPEN𝐌i=h⁡[cos⁡(𝐗⋅𝐑i),sin⁡(𝐗⋅𝐑i),0]),\mathbf{M}_{i}=h\ [\cos(\mathbf{X} \cdot\mathbf{R}_i),\sin(\mathbf{X} \cdot\mathbf{R}_i),0]), (9)

    where 𝐗=(π,−π/3)\mathbf{X}=(\pi,-\pi/\sqrt{3}) i.e., it is translationally invariant along the 𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{2} direction, and alternates between (h,0,0)(h,0,0) and (−h,0,0)(-h,0,0) along the 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} direction. The other two canted-stripe states can also be constructed by taking π/3\pi/3-rotations of the present state (these three states are degenerate in energy). The parameter hh is optimized.

  4. 4.

    Monopole state: Here, no magnetic fields are present and ti​jt_{ij} are complex, with uniform amplitudes and phases that break the translational symmetries of the lattice. The complex phases are chosen so as to have an additional flux of π​Q/N\pi Q/N through every triangular plaquette, where QQ is an integer. A specific gauge choice to generate this flux pattern is given in Ref. [8]. The insertion of this flux leads to Landau levels in the fermionic tight-binding spectrum, specifically 2​Q2Q levels with zero energy for each spin species [39, 8]. Then, by filling all the zero modes for one species (say, up), we obtain a unique state with Sz=QS^{z}=Q. As a consequence, for every magnetization mm, the variational ansatz has no free parameters and, therefore, no optimization is involved. Monopole states are gapless excitations of the Dirac spin liquid, and have been shown to have large overlaps with exact eigenstates of the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model on small clusters [45].

III Results

The phase diagram of the Hamiltonian (1) is determined by optimizing the ansätze described in the previous section using the stochastic-reconfiguration technique within the standard variational Monte Carlo approach [40, 6] and comparing the energies of the optimized states. We denote the variational energy of a given ansatz for an external field HH as

E⁡(Sz,H)=E⁡(Sz,0)−H​Sz.E(S^{z},H)=E(S^{z},0)-HS^{z}. (10)

In fact, since SzS^{z} is a good quantum number of the variational state |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, the Zeeman contribution is simply H​SzHS^{z}. In our simulations, the parameters in each state are optimized to minimize E⁡(Sz,0)E(S^{z},0) for each SzS^{z} sector. Then, the best state for a given HH is the one with the optimal S¯z{\bar{S}^{z}} such that its energy E⁡(S¯z,H)=minSz​{E⁡(Sz,H)}E({\bar{S}^{z}},H)=\text{min}_{S^{z}}\{E(S^{z},H)\}. The magnetization curve is then obtained directly as m⁡(H)=2​S¯z/Nm(H)=2{\bar{S}^{z}}/N.

III.1 Magnetization and scalar spin chirality

We first discuss the case of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model (i.e., J2=0J_{2}=0) to validate the method. Indeed, this model has been studied using spin-wave theory [9, 50], and it is well known that the ground state for a small applied field is the Y phase, which, as the field increases, continuously evolves into the collinear UUD state at magnetization m=1/3m=1/3.

The energies of all ansätze, after optimization, are shown in Fig. 3(a). The energy of the Y state is lower than that of all other cases throughout the entire region of H/J1H/J_{1} investigated. Although the umbrella state has competitive energies, it is never stabilized in our simulations (for any J2J_{2}), in agreement with recent non-linear spin-wave theory and DMRG calculations [4, 27]. The resulting magnetization curve is shown in Fig. 3(b). Our numerical results strongly suggest that the transition from the Y to the UUD plateau is continuous, with no jumps of the magnetization up to m=1/3m=1/3, thus confirming previous results [4, 27].

Next, we discuss the results for larger J2J_{2}, namely J2/J1=0.1J_{2}/J_{1}=0.1, 0.1250.125, and 0.1750.175, see Fig. 4. Remarkably, we find that the monopole states, despite not having tunable parameters, have competitive variational energies throughout the spin-liquid region, lending further support to the underlying Dirac spin liquid in the absence of the external field [24]. At J2/J1=0.1J_{2}/J_{1}=0.1, the system is close to the onset of the monopole phase: although the Y phase remains the lowest in energy, its energy difference from the monopole states is lower than 0.0010.001 up to H/J1≈0.8H/J_{1}\approx 0.8. At J2/J1=0.125J_{2}/J_{1}=0.125, the monopole states have the lowest energy for magnetizations up to slightly above m≈1/6m\approx 1/6, beyond which there is a clear first-order transition to the Y phase. Starting from about J2/J1≈0.16J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.16, the canted-stripe state is stabilized; at J2/J1=0.175J_{2}/J_{1}=0.175, we observe a direct first order transition to the UUD plateau, indicating the end of the stability of the Y phase.

Putting all these results together, we have an estimated phase diagram, see Fig. 1. The monopole phase is stabilized for a significant range of applied field and the J2J_{2} super-exchange. For the 18×1818\times 18 cluster, we estimate that the extent of the phase is 0.1≤J2/J1≤0.160.1\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.16. However, we must mention that, as LL increases, the monopole gap decreases as 1/L1/L [8] and, consequently, the stability range of the monopole phase is expected to broaden with increasing LL.

Our results agree broadly with the predictions of recent spin-wave theory calculations [27, 4], both for the extent of the ordered phases and the nature of the phase transitions between them. Our simple variational wave functions thus prove adequate for capturing the essential physics of the model. We also find excellent agreement between our magnetization curves and DMRG data, see appendix A. The VMC ansatz for the Y phase has only four variational parameters, but achieves an energy comparable to that obtained by DMRG with bond dimension χ=50\chi=50, whose number of variational parameters scales as 𝒪⁡(2​N​χ2)∼𝒪⁡(7×106)\mathcal{O}(2N\chi^{2})\sim\mathcal{O}(7\times 10^{6}).

Finally, the monopole states possess a finite scalar spin chirality (as for the umbrella states). This can be extracted directly from the quantity:

χ=1N​∑[i,j,k]𝐒i⋅(𝐒j×𝐒k),\chi=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{[i,j,k]}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{S}_{j}\times\mathbf{S}_{k}), (11)

where [i,j,k][i,j,k] indicate three nearest-neighbor sites that form an upward triangle in the lattice. The results of the best variational state are reported in Fig. 5 for J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8, where the monopole state is stabilized for H/J1≲1.15H/J_{1}\lesssim 1.15. By contrast, the chirality is identically zero for the Y phase, obtained for H/J1≳1.15H/J_{1}\gtrsim 1.15, since here the spins are coplanar. This result agrees with the one reported in Ref. [42].

III.2 Absence of order in the Monopole phase

We have provided comprehensive numerical evidence that the Dirac spin liquid acquires a finite monopole density in the presence of a magnetic field. This phase was conjectured to have magnetic order in Ref. [33], as a result of the condensation of the monopoles with lattice momentum 𝐪=𝐊\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{K}. Here, we investigate the presence of a possible emergence of magnetic order in the monopole phase by computing the (in-plane) static structure factor:

Sx​y​(𝐪)=1N​∑i,jei​𝐪⋅(𝐑𝐢−𝐑𝐣)​⟨(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)⟩,S^{xy}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\left(\mathbf{R_{i}}-\mathbf{R_{j}}\right)}\langle\left(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}\right)\rangle, (12)

where we sum over all pairs of sites i,ji,j. A phase with magnetic order at 𝐪\mathbf{q} is characterized by a structure factor that grows extensively with system size, i.e., Sx​y​(𝐪)∝NS^{xy}(\mathbf{q})\propto N.

In Fig. 6, we plot Sx​y​(𝐪)S^{xy}(\mathbf{q}) for a finite-density monopole state along with a typical Y and canted-stripe state at the same magnetization. The monopole state is chosen to have magnetization m=1/6m=1/6, which corresponds to an additional flux of π/12\pi/12 through each triangle. For the Y and canted-stripe states, we observe sharp Bragg peaks at the 𝐊/𝐊′\mathbf{K}/\mathbf{K^{\prime}} and 𝐌\mathbf{M} points, respectively. In contrast, the monopole state features much broader signals around the 𝐊\mathbf{K} and 𝐊′\mathbf{K^{\prime}} points, analogous to what is seen in the zero-field Dirac state [24].

In order to understand the ordering characteristics of these different states, we perform a system-size scaling analysis of the Y-ordered state, as well as both the Dirac spin liquid and m=1/6m=1/6 monopole state. We plot the size-scaled in-plane static structure factor Sx​y​(𝐊)/NS^{xy}(\mathbf{K})/N in Fig. 7(a). In the case of the Y-ordered state, we confirm that the Sx​y​(𝐊)/NS^{xy}(\mathbf{K})/N approaches a constant value of 0.026​(2)0.026(2) in the thermodynamic limit. By contrast, in the case of the (zero-field) Dirac spin liquid, we find that the value of the in-plane structure factor Sx​y​(𝐊)S^{xy}(\mathbf{K}) is constant, implying that the scaled quantity Sx​y​(𝐊)/NS^{xy}(\mathbf{K})/N goes to zero as 1/N1/N, see Fig. 7(a).

Turning to the monopole phase, the data appear consistent with the lack of magnetic order on the system sizes considered. The in-plane structure factor Sx​y​(𝐊)/NS^{xy}(\mathbf{K})/N scales to zero, albeit more slowly than the quadratic behavior of the Dirac spin liquid. Although we cannot exclude the possibility that Sx​y​(𝐊)/NS^{xy}(\mathbf{K})/N flattens to a small constant value, we highlight that our results are compatible with other works that suggest the absence of in-plane order  [42].

To better understand the behavior of Sx​y​(𝐊)S^{xy}(\mathbf{K}) in the monopole phase, we study its scaling with magnetization. For small mm, the behavior is dominated by an LL-independent constant, equal to the m=0m=0 Dirac state SDiracx​y​(𝐊)S^{xy}_{\text{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K}). For increasing mm, we observe an additional contribution, which scales with mm and LL. We observe the following empirical scaling law:

Smonox​y​(𝐊)−SDiracx​y​(𝐊)∝mσ​L,S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K})-S^{xy}_{\text{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K})\propto\ m^{\sigma}L, (13)

where we estimate the exponent σ=1.42​(3)\sigma=1.42(3). The scaling collapse found by plotting [Smonox​y​(𝐊)−SDiracx​y​(𝐊)]/L[S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K})-S^{xy}_{\text{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K})]/L, as shown in Fig. 7(b). We interpret the scaling of this quantity in Appendix B, and see this as evidence that the monopole phase is gapless. The in-plane structure factor of the monopole phase Smonox​y​(𝐊)S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K}) has a constant LL-independent Dirac contribution, which is large on small clusters. The finite density of monopoles leads to a divergent contribution in Smonox​y​(𝐊)S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K}). This contribution diverges slower than NN, signaling the absence of magnetic order in the monopole phase. This scaling form is extended to the (relatively large-magnetization) m=1/6m=1/6 state and used to produce the blue fit in Fig. 7(a).

Additionally, the correlations in real space may be considered. To probe magnetic order in the x​yxy plane, we define the spin-spin correlations:

Sx​y​(𝐑max)=⟨S0x​Smaxx⟩+⟨S0y​Smaxy⟩,S^{xy}(\mathbf{R}_{\rm max})=\langle S^{x}_{0}S^{x}_{\rm max}\rangle+\langle S^{y}_{0}S^{y}_{\rm max}\rangle, (14)

where max{\rm max} corresponds to the site at the maximum distance (with periodic-boundary conditions) to the site at the origin of the cluster, specifically 𝐑max=L/2​(𝐚1+𝐚2)\mathbf{R}_{\rm max}=L/2(\mathbf{a}_{1}+\mathbf{a}_{2}). In the inset of Fig. 7(a), we show that these correlations go to zero in the thermodynamic limit, further suggesting the absence of magnetic order in the monopole state.

IV Phase transitions to competing orders: Field theory approach

In this section, we present a complementary theoretical calculation of the stability of the monopole phase against semiclassical Y order. We find that the monopole phase, which emerges continuously from the zero-field U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid, is stable for a large region of the J2−HJ_{2}{-}H phase diagram.

This theoretical calculation of the phase boundary between quantum spin liquid and semiclassical orders follows the method introduced in Ref. [46]. Here, it was shown that transitions to competing semiclassical orders in the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice can be determined self-consistently by the condensation of a fluctuating order parameter [15], called a paramagnon ϕ→​(x)\vec{\phi}(x). From the spin-liquid perspective, it can be seen as a particle-hole bound state of the fractionalized spinons. In the continuum picture, fluctuations of antiferromagnetic order (with ordering wavevector 𝐊\mathbf{K}) are captured with a continuum field theory of this bosonic field [2, 3].

The zero-field transition from the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid to 120∘120^{\circ} coplanar magnetic order is described by the following continuum action:

S=∫d3​x​[|∂tϕ→​(x)|2−c2​|∇ϕ→​(x)|2−α2​r​|ϕ→​(x)|2].S=\int d^{3}x\left[|\partial_{t}\vec{\phi}(x)|^{2}-c^{2}|\bm{\nabla}\vec{\phi}(x)|^{2}-\alpha^{2}r|\vec{\phi}(x)|^{2}\right]. (15)

Thus, the bosonic field has a dispersion ω=Δ2+c2​𝐪2\omega=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+c^{2}\mathbf{q}^{2}}, with a gap Δ2=α2​r\Delta^{2}=\alpha^{2}r for small momenta 𝐪\mathbf{q} around the ordering wavevector. We evaluate this gap self-consistently as a function of the Hamiltonian parameters J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} (i.e., no free parameters). At the critical point r=0r=0, the antiferromagnetic order ϕ→​(x)\vec{\phi}(x) condenses and we get a symmetry-broken state. The boson has linear dispersion ω=c​|𝐪|\omega=c|{\mathbf{q}}| at the critical point Δ=0\Delta=0 and the transition has dynamical exponent z=1z=1. Gauge-field interactions are expected to place it in the QED3 chiral Heisenberg Gross–Neveu universality class [46, 12].

Applying a magnetic field HH breaks S​U​(2)SU(2) spin symmetry, which will split the degeneracy of the paramagnon mode into three SzS^{z} eigenstates, with eigenvalues 0,±10,\pm 1. We now study the instability of the magnetized spin liquid state to semiclassical magnetic ordering, caused by the condensation of the paramagnon. Note that we do not assume anything about the nature of the spin-liquid ansatz in the following, other than the absence of mean-field magnetic order 𝐌i\mathbf{M}_{i} in Eq. (3) before projection. The lowest-energy state ϕ+​(x)\phi_{+}(x) with Sz=+1S^{z}=+1 has an effective action [34]:

S=∫d3x[|(∂t−iH)ϕ+(x)|2−c2|∇ϕ+(x)|2−α2r|ϕ+(x)|2],S=\int d^{3}x\left[|(\partial_{t}-iH)\phi_{+}(x)|^{2}\right.\\ -\left.c^{2}|\bm{\nabla}\phi_{+}(x)|^{2}-\alpha^{2}r|\phi_{+}(x)|^{2}\right], (16)

with dispersion ω=Δ2+c2​𝐪2−H≈(Δ−H)+c2​𝐪2/(2​Δ)\omega=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+c^{2}{\bf q}^{2}}-H\approx(\Delta-H)+c^{2}{\bf q}^{2}/(2\Delta). As such, the semiclassical order condenses at a critical field strength determined by the zero-field paramagnon gap Hc=|Δ|H_{c}=|\Delta|. This assumes that the gap Δ\Delta itself is independent of the field, see Appendix C for details. The resulting transition is like a Bose–Einstein condensation of paramagnons [31, 16]. The condensed magnetic order has the same unit cell as 120∘120^{\circ} order, but an out-of-plane component Sz=+1S^{z}=+1; hence, it is naturally understood as Y order. Interactions are expected to qualitatively modify the z=2z=2 critical point and may drive the transition first order (quartic interactions are marginal and this theory is in the upper critical dimension).

We are interested in describing the phase boundary to Y-order, which corresponds to a closing of the paramagnon gap at the 𝐊\mathbf{K} point. Because there are no low energy fermions at this wavevector, we approximate the ω=0\omega=0 susceptibility of the finite-HH monopole state as equal to the Dirac state. The gap Δ\Delta at the momentum 𝐊\mathbf{K} can be calculated self-consistently in the zero-field Dirac state by integrating out the fermion fluctuations at one-loop level (Appendix C) [46]. We then predict the critical field strength Hc≈|Δ|H_{c}\approx|\Delta| as a function of the Hamiltonian parameters J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1},

Hc/J1≈2.93​2/31−2​J2/J1−0.778,H_{c}/J_{1}\approx 2.93\sqrt{\frac{2/3}{1-2J_{2}/J_{1}}-0.778}, (17)

where the numerical constants are computed on a large system, e.g., with L=720L=720. This calculation is self-consistent, with no free parameters. The critical field strength Hc/J1H_{c}/J_{1} is shown in Fig. 8, showing a good agreement with the VMC method for large fields. Instead, for low fields, we find that the self-consistent field-theoretical method predicts a more stable monopole phase than our VMC results on L=18L=18 clusters. As discussed in Section III.1, this can be understood as being due to finite-size effects in the gapless U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid phase.

Finally, we note that this method cannot be applied so simply to the phase transition to canted stripe order. In this case, the ordering wavevector is at the 𝐌\mathbf{M} point where the zero-field spin liquid has gapless fermion bilinear excitations. As such, the fermion susceptibility and hence the gap of the paramagnon will depend non-trivially on the applied magnetic field. We leave it to future work to understand how this mechanism leads to the stabilization of the monopole phase over canted stripe order. These results confirm that the monopole condensate phase can be stable to semiclassical ordering for intermediate magnetic fields.

V Conclusions

We investigated the triangular Heisenberg model in a magnetic field using variational wave functions and quantum Monte Carlo techniques to optimize the parameters and evaluate the physical quantities [40, 6]. A few relevant ansätze have been analyzed, representing plausible candidate phases for the ground-state phase diagram. In the low-J2J_{2} regime, we recover that the Y state is selected below the m=1/3m=1/3 magnetization plateau, where the gapped UUD state is stabilized. For large J2J_{2}, the canted-stripe state is obtained for small external fields. Most interestingly, in the highly-frustrated regime (i.e., J2/J2≈1/8J_{2}/J_{2}\approx 1/8, where the same approach has predicted the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid at H=0H=0 [24]), we clearly find the existence of a “monopole phase”, described by states in which a finite density of magnetic monopoles are added on top of the Dirac spin liquid.

We provided a self-consistent random-phase approximation (RPA) calculation of the gap to fluctuations of semiclassical Y ordering in this monopole phase, and use it to evaluate a critical field strength that agrees with our VMC calculations. It would be interesting to calculate the instability to (canted) stripe ordering using this method as well, although there exist significant technical challenges in this case, since the semiclassical paramagnon mode sits in the Dirac continuum.

The in-plane structure factor of the monopole phase scales with system size sub-extensively, a fact which points to the absence of magnetic order in the transverse plane (albeit leaves open the possibility of other gapless excitations). This result, which is an incontrovertible property of the variational wave function as constructed here, conflicts with previous theoretical expectations. Of course, we cannot exclude that more refined states, e.g., including linear combinations of monopole configurations at different filling of the zero-energy modes of the auxiliary Hamiltonian, may give a better description of the highly-frustrated regime with H>0H>0. However, a numerical treatment that may include these effects is not easily implemented. The absence of magnetic order in the x​yxy plane and the finite scalar chirality represent the hallmark of this state, which is definitely different from classical umbrella states (possessing finite magnetic order in the x​yxy plane). We believe these results will drive further research into the root of the problem, motivating analytical and numerical calculations on frustrated Heisenberg models, as well as experimental investigations on candidate materials.

Appendix A Benchmarks with the DMRG method

Here, we show a few comparisons between VMC and DMRG calculations. The latter approach works best on cylindrical geometries with large aspect ratios, which will be considered here. In Fig. 9(a), we show the magnetization curve at J2=0J_{2}=0 obtained by VMC and DMRG simulations. We observe excellent agreement between the different curves, lending strong support to our variational ansatz, which describes the Y phase. We note that on the 24×624\times 6 cylinder, the optimized Y ansatz has a variational energy comparable to that of DMRG with bond dimension χ=50\chi=50, which corresponds to around 7×1067\times 10^{6} variational parameters.

In Fig. 9(b), we show a similar comparison at J2=1/8J_{2}=1/8. For our VMC calculations on the 24×624\times 6 cylinder, the monopole phase is never stabilized, and we consequently observe no phase transition. We attribute this to the absence of flux quantization, which is present on a torus. We have verified that a monopole phase is recovered on large asymmetric geometries (e.g., the 72×672\times 6 system), provided that periodic boundary conditions are imposed in both directions. The agreement among the different curves is reasonable, and improves closer to the 1/31/3 plateau.

In addition, we also compare the energies of the VMC and DMRG approaches for different values of the frustrating ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and magnetization, see Table. 1. In this case, the VMC calculations are performed on the 72×672\times 6 cluster (with periodic-boundary conditions along both directions), while the infinite DMRG (iDMRG) algorithm has been used on the YC6 cylinder [48]. Typically, we observe that the accuracy of the VMC calculations is always below 3%3\%. The best cases are obtained in the putative “monopole phase”, giving more support for the phase diagram that we obtained. The worst accuracy corresponds to the stripe phase, where our ansatz breaks the rotational symmetry (on L×LL\times L clusters) and the reflection symmetry on cylindrical geometry.

Appendix B Scaling of in-plane structure factor

Here, we take another look at the data shown in Fig. 7 and discuss the scaling of in-plane structure factor with system size LL and magnetization mm. First of all, we notice that the static structure factor is written in terms of the dynamical one as:

Sx​y​(𝐪)=∫0∞d​ω​Sx​y​(𝐪,ω).S^{xy}(\mathbf{q})=\int_{0}^{\infty}d{\omega}\;S^{xy}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\,. (18)

Whenever the ground state is gapped to some quasiparticle-like excitation at energy ω0>0\omega_{0}>0, the structure factor takes the form S⁡(𝐊,ω)=c​δ​(ω−ω0)+Sinc​(𝐊,ω)S(\mathbf{K},\omega)=c\delta(\omega-\omega_{0})+S_{\text{inc}}(\mathbf{K},\omega), where Sinc​(𝐊,ω)S_{\text{inc}}(\mathbf{K},\omega) is some incoherent part that vanishes for ω<ω0\omega<\omega_{0}. On finite clusters, S⁡(𝐊,ω)S(\mathbf{K},\omega) is finite, with small size effects, such that it converges to a finite value in the thermodynamic limit. Instead, when the system is gapless, the dynamical structure factor possess a continuum, e.g., S⁡(𝐊,ω)≈ω−αS(\mathbf{K},\omega)\approx\omega^{-\alpha}. On a finite-size cluster, this will be regulated by an infrared cutoff, which scales as ωL≈1/L\omega_{L}\approx 1/L. In this case, integrating over frequencies can produce a divergent contribution ωL1−α≈Lα−1\omega_{L}^{1-\alpha}\approx L^{\alpha-1} if α≥1\alpha\geq 1. For 1<α<31<\alpha<3, this divergence is weaker than L2L^{2} and the state is disordered and critical.

Turning to the J1−J2J_{1}{-}J_{2} Heisenberg model, we present the VMC calculations of the in-plane static structure factor as unscaled data in Fig. 10(a). First of all, the structure factor diverges as NN in the Y phase, as discussed in the main text. On the other hand, it goes to a constant in the Dirac state. This is compatible with a finite gap to the paramagnon mode, as discussed in Ref. [46]. We observe that the divergence of the structure factor in the monopole state (with m=1/6m=1/6) behaves as Smonox​y​(𝐊)=SDiracx​y​(𝐊)+c​LS^{xy}_{\mathrm{mono}}(\mathbf{K})=S^{xy}_{\mathrm{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K})+cL, for some constant cc. This behavior is also seen as a function of magnetization in Fig. 10(b). All together, these observations justify the subtraction of a constant Dirac component in the scaling analysis, performed in the main text in Eq. (13). This result suggests an exponent α=2\alpha=2 and a consequently a divergent dynamical structure factor in the monopole phase S⁡(𝐊,ω)∼1/ω2S(\mathbf{K},\omega)\sim 1/\omega^{2}.

Finally, we note that Ref. [33] predicted this monopole phase has a finite in-plane magnetization mx​ym_{xy} due to monopole confinement. Assuming there is a finite in-plane magnetic order parameter, one can predict its scaling as a function of magnetic field HH as follows: The magnetization of the mean-field state scales as m≈H2m\approx H^{2} and, in the Landau level, the magnetization is proportional to the degeneracy of the Landau level itself, i.e., m≈bm\approx b, which is linear in the induced flux density bb. The resulting Landau state has a gapped spectrum with spacing that goes as b≈H\sqrt{b}\approx H; confinement of gauge fluctuations is then expected to lead to a magnetically ordered state. On the triangular lattice, the x​yxy order parameter is related to the monopole expectation value mx​y≈⟨Φ⟩m^{xy}\approx\langle\Phi\rangle and by dimensional analysis, one can then show that the order scales mx​y≈HΔΦm^{xy}\approx H^{\Delta_{\Phi}} where ΔΦ\Delta_{\Phi} is the scaling dimension of the monopole operator at the QED3 fixed point.

Despite our numerical observations pointing to the absence of magnetic order in the monopole phase, we nonetheless observe a power-law dependence of the divergent contribution on the magnetization [Smonox​y​(𝐊)−SDiracx​y​(𝐊)]/L∝mσ[S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K})-S^{xy}_{\text{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K})]/L\propto m^{\sigma} [see Eq. (13)]. In order to compare with the field-theoretic calculation, we must evaluate this quantity as a function of applied field HH, but we highlight that this is made difficult by the large H=0H=0 plateau.

Preliminary calculations on the L=18L=18 cluster point to a scaling [Smonox​y​(𝐊)−SDiracx​y​(𝐊)]/L≈H2.02[S^{xy}_{\text{mono}}(\mathbf{K})-S^{xy}_{\text{Dirac}}(\mathbf{K})]/L\approx H^{2.02}, which is compatible with a critical exponent ΔΦ=1.01​(3)\Delta_{\Phi}=1.01(3). It is curious that this is compatible with the monopole scaling dimension of QED3, despite there being no in-plane order. We leave it up to future work to evaluate this scaling behavior and to either search for very weak in-plane order, or explain why the field-theoretical treatment breaks down.

Appendix C Details of the field-theoretical treatment

C.1 Zero-field

It has been suggested that the finite-energy spectrum of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid is dominated by a sharp spinon-bound state, whose energy Δ\Delta at the 𝐊\mathbf{K} point can be evaluated as a function of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} in a self-consistent random-phase approximation [46]. Tracking the condensation of this mode as the gap closes (Δ→0\Delta\to 0) allowed for the prediction of a critical transition into the 120∘120^{\circ} magnetically ordered phase.

An effective field theory of the spinon bound state can be written in two steps. First, we form an O⁡(3)O(3) field out of the fluctuating order parameters [2, 3]. In our triangular lattice model, we focus on an antiferromagnetic order parameter ϕ→​(𝐱)∼ei​𝐊⋅𝐱​⟨S→⟩\vec{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\sim e^{i\mathbf{K}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\langle\vec{S}\rangle with ordering wavevector 𝐊\mathbf{K}. Next, we work in the parton language and, with the approach of Ref. [46], derive the couplings in the continuum field theory from the lattice model. In practice, we perform a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation on the interacting spin model in the parton picture to decouple the fluctuations of antiferromagnetic order. Then, we move to momentum space and integrate out the fermions, which gives a self-energy correction to the order parameter field at the one-loop level. Focusing on small momenta 𝐪\mathbf{q} around 𝐊\mathbf{K}, the non-linear sigma model reads [46]

S=∑𝐪[−(α𝐊0)2​(J𝐊−1−2​Π𝐊0)+ω2−c2​𝐪2]​|ϕ→𝐪|2,S=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}[-(\alpha^{0}_{\mathbf{K}})^{2}(J_{\mathbf{K}}^{-1}-2\Pi^{0}_{\mathbf{K}})+\omega^{2}-c^{2}{\mathbf{q}}^{2}]|\vec{\phi}_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2}\,, (19)

up to an overall constant. The mean-field gap is given in terms of the Fourier transform of the Heisenberg interaction

J𝐊−1=2/3J1−2​J2.J_{\mathbf{K}}^{-1}=\frac{2/3}{J_{1}-2J_{2}}\,. (20)

The constants 2​Π𝐊0=0.778​J1−12\Pi^{0}_{\mathbf{K}}=0.778\,J_{1}^{-1}, α𝐊0=2.93​J13/2\alpha^{0}_{\mathbf{K}}=2.93\,J_{1}^{3/2} are evaluated numerically from the mean-field of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin-liquid state. They are defined in terms of the non-interacting fermion susceptibility χ0​(𝐪,ω)\chi^{0}({\mathbf{q}},\omega) as

Π𝐊0=[χ0​(𝐪,ω)]𝐪=𝐊,ω=0,\displaystyle\Pi^{0}_{\mathbf{K}}=[\chi^{0}({\mathbf{q}},\omega)]_{{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{K},\omega=0}\,, (21)
α𝐊0=2​[∂2χ0∂ω2]𝐪=𝐊,ω=0−2.\displaystyle\alpha^{0}_{\mathbf{K}}=2\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\chi^{0}}{\partial\omega^{2}}\right]^{-2}_{{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{K},\omega=0}\,. (22)

Here, we have related field-theory parameters to the behavior of the fermion susceptibility. Then, we define:

α2​r=(α𝐊0)2​(J𝐊−1−2​Π𝐊0)=(2.93)2​[2/31−2​J2/J1−0.778]​J1 2,\alpha^{2}r=(\alpha^{0}_{\mathbf{K}})^{2}(J_{\mathbf{K}}^{-1}-2\Pi^{0}_{\mathbf{K}})\\ =(2.93)^{2}\left[\frac{2/3}{1-2J_{2}/J_{1}}-0.778\right]J_{1}^{\ 2}, (23)

and we derive the form

S=∑𝐪[−α2​r+ω2−c2​𝐪2]​|ϕ→𝐪|2.S=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}[-\alpha^{2}r+\omega^{2}-c^{2}{\mathbf{q}}^{2}]|\vec{\phi}_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2}\,. (24)

This leads to a quasiparticle with dispersion

ω=Δ2+c2​𝒒2,\omega=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+c^{2}\bm{q}^{2}}\,, (25)

with mass Δ2=α2​r\Delta^{2}=\alpha^{2}r. The condensation of antiferromagnetic order at 𝐊\mathbf{K} at r=0r=0 is a critical point with dynamical exponent z=1z=1. We write this in real-space in the main text Eq. (15).

C.2 Finite-field

A uniform magnetic field couples to the ferromagnetic component mm. This is different to the antiferromagnetic order parameter field; in Haldane’s non-linear sigma model description, the uniform magnetization is L→=n→×∂tn→\vec{L}=\vec{n}\times\partial_{t}\vec{n}. Adding the term L→2−H→⋅L→\vec{L}^{2}-\vec{H}\cdot\vec{L} and integrating out L→\vec{L} shows that the magnetic field enters as if it were a background gauge field [34]. We define the new modified time derivative

Dt​ϕ→=∂tϕ→−H→×ϕ→.D_{t}\vec{\phi}=\partial_{t}\vec{\phi}-\vec{H}\times\vec{\phi}\,. (26)

One can write this as a background SU(2) gauge field

Dt​ϕa=∂tϕa+i​H​(Tz)a​c​ϕc,D_{t}\phi^{a}=\partial_{t}\phi^{a}+iH(T^{z})_{ac}\phi^{c}\,, (27)

where (Ta)b​c=−i​ϵa​b​c(T^{a})_{bc}=-i\epsilon_{abc} are the SU(2) structure constants and the kinetic term looks like a covariant derivative.

We can now rewrite the 3-component field ϕ→\vec{\phi} in the basis of SzS^{z} and raising/lowering operators. This is to simplify the modified derivative of Eq. (26); we define the fields

ϕ0=ϕz,ϕ±=(ϕx±i​ϕy)/2,\phi_{0}=\phi_{z}\,,\quad\phi_{\pm}=(\phi_{x}\pm i\phi_{y})/\sqrt{2}\,, (28)

such that Tz​ϕ±=±ϕ±T^{z}\phi_{\pm}=\pm\phi_{\pm}. Then the derivative terms simplify to

|∂tϕ0|2+|(∂t−iH)ϕ+|2+|(∂t+iH)ϕ−|2.|\partial_{t}\phi_{0}|^{2}+|(\partial_{t}-iH)\phi_{+}|^{2}+|(\partial_{t}+iH)\phi_{-}|^{2}\,. (29)

The mode ϕ0\phi_{0} has an effective theory much like Eq. (24), but in terms of a single scalar boson. The action for the other two modes takes the form

S=∑𝐪[−α2​r+(ω∓H)2+c2​𝐪2]​|ϕ±|2.S=\sum_{\bf q}[-\alpha^{2}r+(\omega\mp H)^{2}+c^{2}{\bf q}^{2}]|\phi_{\pm}|^{2}\,. (30)

These three fields hence have dispersions with the energy given by

ω0=Δ2+c2​𝒒2,ω±=Δ2+c2​𝒒2∓H.\omega_{0}=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+c^{2}\bm{q}^{2}}\,,\quad\omega_{\pm}=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+c^{2}\bm{q}^{2}}\mp H\,. (31)

The mode ϕ+\phi_{+} with Sz=+1S^{z}=+1 is lowered in energy, and hence will close with a quadratic dispersion. To see this, expand the lower band for small momentum 𝐪{\bf q} away from the minimum at 𝑲\bm{K}

ω+​(𝐪)≈(Δ−H)+c2​𝐪22​Δ.\omega_{+}({\bf q})\approx(\Delta-H)+\frac{c^{2}{\bf q}^{2}}{2\Delta}. (32)

We can define a chemical potential

μ=Δ−H=α​r−H\mu=\Delta-H=\alpha\sqrt{r}-H (33)

which controls the transition. When μ=0\mu=0, the mode condenses with quadratic dispersion; as such the theory now has a dynamical exponent z=2z=2. Our RPA calculation Eq. (23) allows us to define a critical field-strength Hc=|Δ|H_{c}=|\Delta| as a function of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. This is discussed in the main text and plotted in Fig. 8. To do this, we make a fundamental assumption that the parameter Δ\Delta is independent of field strength. We expect this to hold for this theory of the transition between the spin liquid state and Y magnetic order, since the fermion spectrum is gapped at the 𝐊\mathbf{K} point. This means the real part of the fermion susceptibility at zero frequency is well approximated as independent of the field strength. Note that to describe the transition to canted stripe order, this approximation will not hold and we must calculate the field-dependent susceptibility of the Dirac cones. We expect that these effects will act to further stabilize the monopole state for the following reason: introducing a gap to the Dirac cone will lower the fermion susceptibility at ω=0\omega=0. A reduction in Π𝐌0\Pi^{0}_{\mathbf{M}} as a function of HH will in turn lead to an increase in rr, stabilizing the paramagnons. This sketch should be confirmed with quantitative calculations which is beyond the scope of the current work.
